extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical mechanics (advanced undergraduates/graduates), historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the classical mechanics principles governing impacts and collisions (elastic and inelastic), including assumptions, conservation laws, constructive proofs, and applied measurement methods (e.g., ballistic pendulum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between pressure and momentum (force of percussion vs pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The force of percussion (momentum, impulse, quantity of motion m v) is a quantity of different dimensions from pressure p; pressure and momentum are fundamentally different physical quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains by dimensional argument: the dimensions of momentum (m·l/t) differ from those of pressure. Describes qualitatively why instantaneous impact (percussion) cannot be counteracted by a static pressure notion and why introducing a static value a/is is inadmissible in the dynamical case; relates to measurement of impact of a continuous fluid jet by comparing momentum destroyed per second with pressure acting per second.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring impact of a continuous fluid jet by pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous fluid jet's impact can be measured by the pressure it exerts because one compares the momentum destroyed per second with the pressure acting per second — making the compared quantities homogeneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that for a continuous jet you compare 'momentum destroyed per second' with 'pressure per second', i.e., homogeneous quantities; places this in context of Galileo's experiments and the correct dynamical (not static) conception of how effluent particles generate velocity via mutual pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wallis's momentum-based rule for inelastic impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisive factor in impact is the momentum (product of mass and velocity). For inelastic bodies: if two inelastic bodies have equal momenta they come to rest after impact; if unequal, the difference is the momentum after impact; dividing this momentum by the sum of masses yields the post-impact common velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives Wallis's constructive rule and the commonly used formula u = (m v + m' v')/(m + m'), with explanation that this follows from considering internal form-altering forces and using conservation of quantity of motion for the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Huygens's assumptions for elastic collisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Huygens proceeds from five assumptions: (i) the law of inertia; (2) that equal elastic bodies with equal and opposite velocities separate with the same velocities after impact; (3) that all velocities are relatively estimated; (4) that a larger body striking a smaller one at rest imparts velocity to the latter and loses part of its own; (5) that if one colliding body preserves its velocity, the other does too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions are the foundation of Huygens's derivations; they are partly empirical (existence of elastic bodies) and partly methodological (use of relative velocities and moving reference frames, e.g., the boat thought experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal elastic masses exchange velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: For two equal elastic masses colliding with equal and opposite velocities, they rebound with exactly the same velocities (i.e., they exchange velocities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens justifies this by a boat thought experiment: viewed from a moving frame the collision reduces to one mass at rest struck by the other, leading to the conclusion that equal elastic masses exchange velocities; this is asserted as a principle grounded in experience of elastic bodies regaining form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative velocity of approach equals relative velocity of separation (elastic case)
rubrics_metrics.description: In elastic collisions the relative velocity of approach before impact equals the relative velocity of separation after impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived using the boat (moving-frame) fiction and, for general masses, shown via considerations of vis viva and symmetry. This principle is used to deduce general formulae of elastic collisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of quantity of motion (momentum) in impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The algebraic sum of the momenta of a system of moving bodies is preserved in impact (both elastic and inelastic) when velocities are reckoned with sign in a chosen direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies Descartes' earlier notion: although momenta of individual bodies can 'vanish' in a Cartesian sense, the signed sum is preserved; used to derive formulas for common velocity after inelastic collisions and the general momentum equations for collisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of vis viva (kinetic energy) in perfectly elastic collisions; loss in inelastic collisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The vis viva (sum of m v^2) of a system of perfectly elastic masses is preserved in impact; for inelastic masses vis viva is diminished by an amount equal to the work done by internal (molecular) forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huygens observed vis viva conservation for elastic collisions; the text gives Carnot's form for the loss of vis viva and interprets the loss as the work performed by internal forces, with algebraic expressions for the loss and equivalence between formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling elastic impact requires deformation-dependent restitution forces and impenetrability
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat elastic impact one must recognize that deformation of elastic bodies produces restitution forces that depend directly on the deformation; bodies also possess impenetrability, so contact forces act until velocities equalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how Newtonian principles with the additional empirical observation about elastic deformation lead to Huygens's results; during contact internal forces equalize velocities and then restore form, producing the rebound governed by conservation laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forces of impact are determined by differences of velocity; reference-frame independence (boat fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: All forces of impact are determined by differences of velocity (relative velocities); choice of the reference body for estimating velocities is indifferent — fictitious uniform translations do not affect impact results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes Huygens's successful use of fictitious motions: by adding a uniform translation (boat velocity) many distinct-looking cases reduce to the same case. Analogy drawn between velocity as a physical 'level' and temperature/potential; demonstrates that only velocity differences (or their squares) matter for impact/energy effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: No instantaneous forces — use impulse (integral of force over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the notion of truly instantaneous forces; impacts involve very large but finite forces acting over very short intervals — therefore use the impulse ∫F dt to relate force to momentum change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in the ballistic pendulum reasoning: if force during impact is not constant, replace Ft by ∫F dt; momentum change equals impulse; Poncelet's warning against instantaneous-force concepts is cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballistic pendulum as a method to determine projectile velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: A projectile's velocity can be determined by capturing it in a pendulum mass and using conservation of momentum (for the impact) and energy (pendulum rise) to relate projectile mass and pendulum oscillation to the shot velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents two derivations: (a) simple pendulum approximation V^2 = 2gh = (gT/π)^2(1−cos α) and v ≈ (M/m) V for small m; (b) torque/impulse method using point of percussion, moments and angular impulse leading to formula v = (2 M a / m b^2)^{1/2} · (gT)^{1/2} · sin(α/2) (forms shown). Lists required observations: masses (m, M), distances of centre of gravity and point of percussion from axis, time and extent of oscillation; notes agreement between both derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center of percussion for rotating bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rotating body whose motion is suddenly checked by arresting one of its points, the intensity of percussion (impact) varies with the distance of the arrested point from the axis; the point of greatest intensity is the centre of percussion — if this point is checked the axis sustains no pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed to Wallis; mentioned as important in rotational-impact problems and machine parts, but detailed developments are elsewhere; concept used in ballistic pendulum torque reasoning (distance b from axis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive partition method for deriving momentum conservation (graphical/constructive proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of proving the momentum-sum rule by partitioning masses and combining collisions of equal parts progressively until the total system attains a common velocity, showing (m + m') u = m v + m' v'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the constructive geometric reasoning (represent masses as line segments, velocities as ordinates), cutting off portions and successively equalizing velocities to arrive at the surface equation of momentum conservation; emphasizes that some prior experiential notion of mv as the decisive form is needed to pursue this reasoning without Newtonian principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-impact simplification vs oblique impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating colliding masses as point particles moving along the line joining their centres (direct impact) is admissible when centres of gravity and the contact point are collinear; oblique impact is more complicated but introduces no new principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that earlier expositions treat impacts as one-dimensional (direct); oblique impacts require more elaborate analysis (including rotational effects), but are conceptually reducible to the same Newtonian principles.
